### C-R4-01
- **Claim:** Goldingay divides Jer 7–24 as **Part Two** of the scroll, introduced by third-person “the message that came to Jeremiah from Yahweh” at 7:1; 11:1; 14:1; 18:1; 21:1—contrasting the first-person form of 2:1 (basically the 604 scroll)—so Part Two issues from curators’ collating work, presumably after 587.
- **Quote:** “As Jer 2–6 began Yahweh’s message came to me, a similar phrase in the third person occurs in 7:1 and will recur in 11:1; 14:1; 18:1; 21:1. … Whereas the first-person form in 2:1 makes sense if Jer 2–6 is basically the 604 scroll, this use of the third-person form makes sense if what follows issues from the collating work of Jeremiah’s curators, presumably after 587.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 1–6; intro to Part Two (7:1–24:10)
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R4-02
- **Claim:** Within Part Two, **Part 2a** is 7:1–10:25 (“Exhortations and Exchanges”); 7:1–15 links chronologically just before 604, while 10:1–25 suggests after 597; 7:1–8:3 is five prose exhortations/confrontations/warnings about **worship**.
- **Quote:** “While Jer 7:1–15 links chronologically with the period just before 604 (see the comment), 10:1–25 suggests a time after 597. … All five sections concern unacceptable worship that earns Yahweh’s wrath and leads to banishment.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 10–66; outline of Part 2a / 7:1–8:3
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R4-03
- **Claim:** Goldingay outlines five worship units in 7:1–8:3: (1) worship without community truthfulness (7:1–15); (2) Queen of the Heavens (7:16–20); (3) worship without life by Yahweh’s bidding (7:21–28); (4) child sacrifice (7:29–34); (5) sun/moon/stars (8:1–3)—each half moves from wayward attitudes accompanying Yahweh-worship to worship wayward in how/to whom it is offered.
- **Quote:** “While the specific subject changes for each section, only the first and third have introductions … Each half begins with worship of Yahweh that is accompanied by wayward attitudes and moves on to worship that is itself wayward in how or to whom it is offered.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 40–72; on 7:1–8:3 structure
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R4-04
- **Claim:** Goldingay identifies 7:2–15 as the report of the **temple sermon** whose narrative context is Jer 26, set at “the beginning of the reign of king Jehoiakim” (~609/608)—about four years before the 604 scroll; if Jer 2–6 is basically that scroll, either “all the words” (36:2) need not be taken too literally or Jer 7 and 26 are more like imaginative creations by the curators than historical accounts.
- **Quote:** “Jeremiah 26 relates how Jeremiah delivered such a message … Jeremiah 7:2–15 is thus a report of that message. Jeremiah 26 sets its story in ‘the beginning of the reign of king Jehoiakim,’ about 609 or 608 and some four years before the writing of the 604 scroll. If Jer 2–6 more or less comprises that scroll, either the command that the scroll contain ‘all the words that I have spoken to you’ (36:2) need not be taken too literally, or Jer 7 and 26 are more like imaginative creations by the curators than historical accounts.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 123–125; on 7:1–15 / Jer 26
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R4-05
- **Claim:** Reception-history function of the temple sermon: in 609 and following decades it urges change of community life to forestall temple destruction (cf. 26:1–3); after 587 it explains that event; after 516 its message about community life and not trusting possession of the temple becomes important again.
- **Quote:** “In the context of 609 and the next decades, the sermon would urge people toward a change of community life that would forestall the temple destruction, as 26:1–3 suggests. After 587, it would explain that event. After 516, its message about community life and not trusting in possession of the temple would again become important.”
- **Locus:** slice l. 125; on 7:1–15 reception
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R4-06
- **Claim:** Goldingay stresses “place” (māqôm) as load-bearing: locus of encounter, scene of living rightly, and link between Yahweh’s destruction of Shiloh and threatened destruction of the Jerusalem place; in Jer 7 “place” “carries the weight of ambivalence” (temple vs land/city).
- **Quote:** “Jeremiah—book and prophet—foregrounds ‘place’ as locus of encounter between God and people, and as the scene of living rightly with all that implies for the relationship of this people, this place, and this God.” … “In Jer 7, place ‘carries the weight of ambivalence.’”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 125, 161; on 7:1–15 / v. 3
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R4-07
- **Claim:** On 7:4, Goldingay reads triple “Yahweh’s palace” (hêkāl, not mere “temple”) as near-incantation / lucky-charm security rhetoric after Josiah’s death—fallacious self-deception; there is nothing wrong with the conviction that the temple is Yahweh’s palace, but people cannot come into his palace unless paths/practices are made good; Yahweh is prepared to let his palace be destroyed rather than have them think it guarantees security.
- **Quote:** “The ‘temple’ is Yahweh’s house … and it is his palace, his house fit for a king. … ‘This is the house of the real King. The fact that the real King has his palace here means we do not have to fear the king of Babylon.’ But the repetition almost sounds like a lucky charm phrase or an incantation. … Yahweh is prepared to let his palace be destroyed rather than have them think that in itself it guarantees their security.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 163–165; on 7:4
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R4-08
- **Claim:** Goldingay notes Jeremiah “gives no details about the temple” or physical demarcation of space (contrast Ezekiel’s spatial boundaries), which facilitates Christian adaptation: deceptive “Here is the temple of the Lord” applied to claiming one is God’s temple without corrected conduct.
- **Quote:** “Jeremiah gives no details about the temple” and “gives no details here of the land and very little elsewhere. In fact, he shows little interest in the physical demarcation of space.” He contrasts with Ezekiel… “If you have not corrected what you are doing, then you are no temple of God, and God will not save you on account of the sacredness of his temple that is desecrated by you.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 165–165; on 7:4 Christian reception
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R4-09
- **Claim:** On 7:5–7, making paths/practices good means (1) exercise authority between individual and fellow; (2) not defraud resident alien, fatherless, widow; (3) not pour out blood of the guilt-free; (4) not go after other gods—effectively the two great commands; Jeremiah functions as teacher of Torah; security lies in walking Yahweh’s ways, not merely in the Great King’s palace.
- **Quote:** “In effect, vv. 5 and 6 are talking about fulfilling the two great commands, about loving one’s neighbor and loving Yahweh. And Jeremiah is functioning as a teacher of Torah. … People do have a basis of security, but it doesn’t lie simply in the presence of the Great King’s palace; it lies in their commitment to walking his ways.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 169–169; on 7:5–7
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R4-10
- **Claim:** On 7:8–11, the second facet of deceptive words is assuming temple confidence while practicing theft/murder/adultery/false swearing/offerings to the Master/other gods; people then stand in the house over which Yahweh’s name is proclaimed and (ironically) say “We have been rescued in order to do all these offensive things”; the house has become a robbers’ cave in their eyes—Yahweh is not blind; Jesus reuses the words differently (Mark 11:15–17).
- **Quote:** “They say (in the course of their worship in this temple), ‘We have been rescued.’ … ‘The long question, begun in v. 9’ comes to a ‘provocative conclusion with the final clause’: in order to do all these offensive things. … Their behavior therefore makes them no different from a band of robbers hiding up in a cave. … Jesus picks up Jeremiah’s words and takes them in a different direction (Mark 11:15–17).”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 171–173; on 7:8–11
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R4-11
- **Claim:** On Shiloh (7:12–15): Yahweh claims responsibility for destroying the former central sanctuary where he first had his name dwell (Deut language); if he did that once, he will treat Jerusalem’s palace the same; critique basis shifts from ignoring priestly Torah (vv. 3–10) to not listening to prophetic message (cf. 6:19); Ephraim’s throwing-out is the warning.
- **Quote:** “Shiloh … had once been the location of Israel’s central sanctuary and of the pledge chest … but it had been destroyed—we don’t know when or how. Yahweh here claims responsibility for the destruction as an act of retribution in the face of my people Israel’s direness. … Whereas in vv. 3–10, the basis for critique was people’s ignoring the teaching of priests based on established Torah, here the basis for critique is people’s not listening to the message of prophets.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 175–179; on 7:12–15
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R4-12
- **Claim:** Goldingay reads Yahweh’s Shiloh–Zion logic against Ps 78’s “self-serving Jerusalem ideology” (abandon Shiloh, choose Zion), inverted here; originally unconditional love becomes conditional once they belong—unfaithfulness imperils the relationship; parallel warning for the church via Rom 11:21.
- **Quote:** “That story could function as a ‘self-serving Jerusalem ideology.’ Yahweh turns that possibility on its head. The logic will be taken up by Paul in Rom 9–11 … When Yahweh entered into a relationship with Israel, it was not because Israel satisfied certain conditions … But once they belonged to him, their relationship with him required their living faithfully with him and with one another, and unfaithfulness imperiled the relationship. Maybe one should therefore say that his originally unconditional relationship with them becomes conditional.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 177–177; on 7:13–14
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[divine-human-marriage]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R4-13
- **Claim:** On 7:16–20 (prayer prohibition / Queen of the Heavens): Goldingay treats “do not plead” as preaching rhetoric, not permanent ban—reporting the prohibition is an attempt to get through to people; Jer 37 and 42 imply Jeremiah didn’t take it literally/permanently; repetition (11:14; 14:11) may imply he never stopped praying; the “dire command” may all the while imply its opposite.
- **Quote:** “If the prohibition and Jeremiah’s reporting of it are thus part of an attempt to get through to the people, there need be no implication that Jeremiah is being actually or permanently forbidden to pray. Certainly Jer 37 and 42 imply that he didn’t take the prohibition literally, or that he didn’t do so permanently; the subsequent repetition of the injunction (11:14; 14:11) may imply that he never stopped praying. Indeed, perhaps the ‘dire command’ that Jeremiah should not pray is ‘all the while implying its opposite…. Is not a plea implied in the command to cease and desist? In effect: Do not give up on this people!’”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 232–232; on 7:16
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R4-14
- **Claim:** Queen-of-the-Heavens worship (7:17–18) is family/homely spirituality involving children, fathers, women making loaves—throughout towns and streets, not temple; “Queen of the Heavens” is an all-purpose title that could cover any chief goddess; either Josiah’s reformation didn’t reach family spirituality or the message reflects revival of practices Josiah terminated (cf. 44:15–25).
- **Quote:** “Understood positively, this worship was a homely, family affair that gave women a role that they didn’t have in temple worship. … ‘Queen of the Heavens’ is an all-purpose title like ‘Lord’; it could be applied to a chief goddess in a number of different religious systems. … either Josiah’s reformation didn’t reach family spirituality or the message reflects the revival of practices that Josiah terminated.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 234–234; on 7:17–18
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R4-15
- **Claim:** On 7:21–28 (Yahweh’s priorities): Goldingay reads “add whole offerings to fellowship sacrifices and eat meat” as priest-parody scorn—not principled rejection of sacrifice (cf. positive sacrifice texts later in Jeremiah)—hyperbolically stressing that at the exodus/Sinai what Yahweh first ordered was “Listen to my voice” and mutual people/God relationship, not offerings.
- **Quote:** “You can keep both of them, Yahweh says. Eat meat. It’s just a meal. Enjoy your steak, kiddo. There’s nothing religious or sacred about it. … Even in this chapter, his reference to his name being proclaimed in the temple … indicate that he is not in principle dismissive of its worship. … Yahweh again speaks hyperbolically. … To go in the entire path that I order you does not have its focus on sacrifices; what Yahweh wants is that they should listen.”

### C-R4-16
- **Claim:** Goldingay’s worship-critique synthesis for 7:21–28: without discipline/truthfulness outside worship, worship means nothing; scriptural story shows truthfulness is first priority; “my servants the prophets” is distinctively Jeremianic and consistently characterizes Israel as stubbornly rebellious; truthfulness “has perished” and “cut itself off from their mouth.”

The argument here is that the scriptural story shows that God sees truthfulness as the first priority; without it, worship means nothing. … Truthfulness has perished. It has died.”

### C-R4-17
- **Claim:** On 7:29–34 (child sacrifice at Topheth/Ben-Hinnom): Goldingay distinguishes “passing through fire” (2 Kgs 23:10) as possible non-lethal dedication/ordeal from Jeremiah’s incineration language (šārap, everyday burning of remains, not proper sacrificial qāṭar); people may have thought they offered children to Yahweh, but 19:5 / 32:35 name the Master / Molek; “which I did not order; it did not arise in my mind.”
- **Quote:** “When 2 Kgs 23:10 refers only to passing one’s children through fire … it may imply only a dedication ceremony that does not involve their death … Here the rite involves parents offering children in sacrifice. … To sacrifice your child is an ultimate sacrifice that parents were prepared to make when they were under pressure … which I did not order; it did not arise in my mind.”

### C-R4-20
- **Claim:** Jer 8–9 is a new poetic compilation whose distinctive feature is **spirited exchanges** among Yahweh, Judah, and Jeremiah—“polyphonic” scroll, voices in dialogue but talking past each other/interrupting; unannounced speaker shifts reflect “chaos … of traumatic contemplation” and a situation of conflict; all three voices are as Jeremiah articulates them.

### C-R4-23
- **Claim:** On 8:18–9:1, Goldingay attributes the grief-with-the-people voice primarily to **Jeremiah** (not God suffering with people at that hinge), while Yahweh’s “I wish I had a travelers’ lodging” (9:2) is disgust/desire to abandon adulterous people—cosmetic hinge from sympathy to disgust; dual identification (prophet with people and with Yahweh) is key rhetoric.

### C-R4-29
- **Claim:** Goldingay deliberately translates bərît as **“pledge” not “covenant”**: “covenant” carries deceptive theological/US cultural freight of mutuality; a bərît is a solemnly made commitment that can be one-party obligation—here the commitment Yahweh **imposed** on Israel after the exodus (ordered, not mutual contract identity).
- **Quote:** “Pledge is the word bәrît. I avoid the traditional translation ‘covenant,’ which carries deceptive freight; pledge has the advantage of not being a technical theological term. … Second, bәrît does not suggest mutuality. A bәrît is a solemnly made commitment. While it can be made by two parties to one another, it can also be made by one party to another or required as an obligation by one party of another. … In this passage, the bәrît is a solemn commitment or obligation that Yahweh imposed on Israel as a consequence of his getting the people out of Egypt.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 2098–2102; intro to 11:1–17
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[divine-human-marriage]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R4-30
- **Claim:** Goldingay distinguishes: the bərît (imposed obligation) is **part of** a mutual relationship (become people for me / God for you) but is **not identical** with that mutual relationship; in broad sense Jeremiah does think of something like a **marriage covenant or adoption covenant**, though he rarely uses bərît (elsewhere 14:21; 22:9; 50:5; 31:31–34:22).
- **Quote:** “The bәrît is thus part of a mutual relationship in that Israel’s living by this commitment will open up the possibility that it might become a people for Yahweh and he might become God for it. … Yet the relationship between Yahweh and Israel that he regularly presupposes is a solemnly committed mutual relationship … In that broad sense, he does think in terms of something like a marriage covenant or adoption covenant.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 2102–2102; on bərît and relationship
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[divine-human-marriage]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R4-31
- **Claim:** Communicative reason for bərît language in ch. 11: Judah knew Deuteronomic bərît talk and Josiah’s “bərît scroll” (2 Kgs 23:2–3), and knew imperial Assyrian/Babylonian bərît imposed on them—so “You know Assyria laid a bərît on us? Well, so did Yahweh… How much more danger have we risked by ignoring Yahweh’s bərît.” Jeremiah thinks of bərît relationship **politically**.
- **Quote:** “For Deuteronomy, for 2 Kings 23, and for Jer 11:1–17, then, talk in terms of Yahweh’s bәrît could say to people, ‘You know Assyria laid a bәrît on us? Well, so did Yahweh. And you know how dangerous it would have been to ignore the Assyrian bәrît? How much more danger have we risked by ignoring Yahweh’s bәrît.’ So Jeremiah thinks of the relationship between Yahweh and Israel quite broadly but will think of the bәrît relationship in particular politically.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 2104–2104; on 11:1–17 politics of bərît

### C-R4-37
- **Claim (priority — confessions as rhetoric, not diary):** Goldingay rejects the label **“Jeremiah’s confessions”** for 11:18–12:17 even if meant to recall Augustine: Jeremiah does little confession of sin or of Yahweh’s greatness, and is not sharing spiritual autobiography; 20th-c. “lamenting prophet” reading appeals to “the modern self” and lectionaries focused on life over message—but the aim remains persuading Judah to turn.

In the twentieth century, these ‘confessions’ came to be treated as key to an understanding of the Jeremiah scroll; ‘the lamenting prophet’ came to be understood in a way that appeals to ‘the modern self,’ and the reading of Jeremiah in church lectionaries came to focus more on his life than on his message.”
